utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Shall we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Just before the witness is brought back in, I would like to mention something with respect to the 50th motion for disclosure violation, which is presently being considered by the Trial Chamber. You will recall that the Prosecution, in their response, indicated that they were in the process of identifying an additional potential Rule 68 material relating to witness interviews that had been done by the Office of the Prosecutor that may not have been disclosed in a timely fashion by the Trial Chamber's March 31st dead-line, and they attached a transcript of one such interview. And I want to inform the Trial Chamber that in the last few days, we have now received 56 additional items that appear to be violations of Rule 68, and they're of great length. There are many witness interviews, some of which are not transcribed and are hours and hours of tape-recorded interview. Others are transcripts that run into the hundreds of pages. And so I wanted to make you aware of that. We have a pending motion to suspend the trial because of these disclosure violations. And at the time this arose, in your absence, with the revelation of an interview with Mr. Cizmovic, we thought that it may have been the tip of the iceberg, and, indeed, we're seeing the rest of the iceberg now. So we are in a position where we have a huge number of items that take a long time to review, that have just been disclosed to us, and we would like you to take that into consideration when you're deliberating on the suspension of the proceedings as well as the issue of appointing a special master. We intend to file a written motion for the 51st disclosure violation motion, but it's probably going to take three to four weeks before we have reviewed all the video material so that we could point out what exculpatory nature of the material is and how we're prejudiced by each individual violation. But in the meantime, I wanted you to be aware that we have received all of this new material, and it has an impact on our being able to continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. It's well noted. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson. Very well, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Excellency. [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to the paragraph 57 in your report, where you say: [In English] "Of all the various forces within the crisis staffs dealt -- which the crisis staffs dealt, it is in military matters that we see the greatest variety of patterns. One pattern does not describe the whole range of relations between the crisis staffs and the military forces." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] 67.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further down in paragraph 73, you say: [In English] "Tensions could arise, however, in those places where municipal SDS leaders felt that the JNA was not sufficiently supporting their cause, and the JNA Command was suspicious of the military pretensions of the crisis staffs." [Interpretation] Right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 74: [In English] "Some crisis staffs took a different tack: rather than co-operate with the existing military structure, they were involved in arming of local Serbs and the formation of Serb units ..." [Interpretation] And so on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you provide documents showing that crisis staffs formed any units outside the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't referring to the VRS. I was referring to the time before the VRS was formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the Territorial Defence and Civilian Protection; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it was formed outside of the JNA or the existing Territorial Defence structures, some of these Serb units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that according to the law, Territorial Defence and Civilian Protection belong to the municipality, regardless of the JNA? Have you seen -- did you see on Thursday the Law on All People's Defence? It is obviously within the jurisdiction of the municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on Wednesday we saw the Law on All People's Defence. It is within the jurisdiction of the municipal authorities. But this sort of thing, I do have several documents that show that the SDS was forming units outside of the municipal TO or the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that, but we should bear in mind the law that you did not take into account. Let us look at paragraph 79: [In English] "Some cries staffs did, indeed, explicitly distance themselves from direct military command." [Interpretation] And you give some examples. And in paragraph 81. [In English] "Other crisis staffs were also prepared to interpret the government and party instructions in a manner that gave them command authority." [Interpretation] And then in 90: [In English] "As the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff put it, 'The Crisis Staff reviewed the work of the SJB. The Crisis Staff concluded that it does not have the right to interfere with the professional work of the police and army.'" And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What paragraph was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And 91: [In English] "Other crisis staffs were much more assertive in their authority over the Serb police forces." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thus, in some municipalities it is one way, and in other municipalities it is another way, so things vary from municipality to municipality; correct? Both with regard to the army, and with regard to the police, and to the Territorial Defence and the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that within discussion -- discussing the army, that is, the JNA, TO, VRS, there's a spectrum with considerable variation upon it. I say that with regards to the police, there's a more consistent pattern because, for one thing, the commander of the police was always a part of the Crisis Staff. So there are distinctions, as I see, between Kotor Varos -- the statement from Kotor Varos and what we see in some other places about the extent of their interference in the execution of the police tasks, but I see the relationship as much closer and consistent with the police than with the other armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many municipalities have you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed the documents that we have in our -- in evidence. For some municipalities, we have a great deal of documentary evidence. For others, we have only a very scanty collection. Some, we have none at all. So I would have to count through. You can see in my footnotes I bolded the name of each municipality for ease, and I -- just sort of going through the footnotes, we could go through and count. But I really couldn't say, off the top of my head, how many municipalities I had actually documents from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I then assist you, perhaps? Is that 10, 15 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it 20? Let's begin with the west, Novi Grad. You took that into consideration; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the former Bosanski Novi or Sarajevo Novi Grad? I did both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi. Bosanski Novi, Prijedor - I'll enumerate - Sanski Most, Kljuc, Banja Luka? Did you take Banja Luka into account?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a few documents of a Banja Luka municipal Crisis Staff. I didn't have many of those. It was hard to distinguish between the ARK Crisis Staff and the Banja Luka municipal authorities. But I do have something from the Banja Luka War Presidency, so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Krupa, Petrovac -- Bosanska Krupa, Petrovac, Sanski Most. In the middle municipalities, that's Bosanski Brod, Brcko, Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brcko and Bijeljina, I had documents. Bosanski Brod, I'm not sure I did. Only one or two, if I found anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good. Do you know how many municipalities there were in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska, no, I don't. As I said, there were about 100 and -- between 100 and 110 municipalities in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know how many -- presumably fewer in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you accept that with the newly-established municipalities -- entire municipalities that were not divided and the newly-established municipalities, Republika Srpska had 61 or 62 municipalities, but there were 55 major large municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems quite possible, but I have no basis for -- I never counted them in that way, so I have no basis for agreeing or disagreeing. It seems likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you perhaps took into account one-third or perhaps one half of all municipalities and studied them, and within that framework, you were not able to establish a pattern. Why didn't you take into account the other municipalities? If it is about state policy of persecuting a minority population coming from the central level, from a powerful leader or an authoritarian regime, as your predecessor called them, if it's state policy, it is applied in the entire republic, whereas you did not manage to find and determine a pattern even in this limited number of municipalities. Why did you not review all the municipalities to tell us what those central authorities did?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I am limited by the evidence in the possession of the OTP. I reviewed the evidence available to me as thoroughly as possible. There were many municipalities where evidence was never collected. I have noted throughout my report that I'm limited to the evidence available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say the Prosecution did not take into account the entire territory of Republika Srpska, that it did not investigate what happened in Srbac, for instance? Have you heard of that municipality, Srbac?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that municipality, some Muslims remained to live together with us, they were in the army, they were well respected, and there was not a single problem? Did you investigate -- did you research why?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that some Muslims remained in Srbac. I am not -- I have no basis to say how well respected they were or that there was not a single problem. I did not -- I was unable to investigate Srbac because there was no evidence available to me on Srbac. I didn't have access to the Crisis Staff minutes, or decisions, or the Municipal Gazette of Srbac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you saying that they did not give evidence to you, or was there no evidence? Did the OTP ever investigate things and see -- in Srbac in order to find whether the Serbs there were guilty of any sins? I'm asking you about Srbac, but I'm not limiting myself to that. They made your selection for you, and you, in your turn, were even more selective and you narrowed down your research to some documents which do not portray a very clear picture, they do not reflect what you purport to say in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are many questions that you've asked. Do you want me to take them in order or just answer the last one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's in your hands, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All right. "They" did not -- who are "they"? I have complete access to all the evidence in the possession of the OTP. Their evidence is limited to where they investigated and collected evidence or what evidence they have received from other sources. Nobody limited my access to anything. I had access to everything there is here. I did not go out into the field and collect evidence of non-investigated -- uninvestigated municipalities. I believe they did not investigate Srbac because they did not hear of crimes committed there. The OTP's mandate is to investigate crimes, not to investigate the entire history of every municipality in the Republika Srpska. That there were some places where crimes did not occur does not alter the crimes that did occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, you are trying to establish a link between the central authorities and the chaotic events that happened during the civil war. Why didn't you list any of the municipalities where crimes did not happen, and why didn't you say, then, these people did not listen to what Karadzic was saying or Karadzic did not instigate any crimes there? You're talking about central authorities. The president of a republic is on trial here, and the OTP is trying to prove that what was happening during the case of a civil war was something that the central authorities were behind. Why didn't you take into account so many municipalities where nothing of the sort happened?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not say -- I do not say that Karadzic instigated crimes here. I say that crisis staffs considered themselves part of the Bosnian Serb state system and took orders and instructions from the central organs from the republican level. And I do, indeed, cite in my footnotes some municipalities where, as far as I know, crimes have never been charged, simply because they provided evidence of the links, not of links that had to do with crimes, but simply links. For example, Bosanska Dubica, Bosanska Gradiska, I had their municipal gazettes. I don't know how those came into the possession of the OTP, but they were there, I looked at them and I saw that they received Djeric's instructions, formed crisis staffs, recognised the republican authority. I also see that those crisis staffs, in municipalities where there was a large-scale moving out of population, that they did it with such a similar pattern that it's hard to believe it was spontaneous that they all formed these agencies, that they all met and said, Let's move out our Muslims; not all of them, but the seven municipalities. But I see enough co-ordination between municipalities on the issue of moving out and I see instructions and communications on various topics from the republican level to the municipality that I concluded that there was -- that the crisis staffs operated as part of a state system and that there appears to be, among the municipalities, a co-ordinated policy of moving out the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, let me put it this way: You stated that there was some places where crimes did not occur, does not alter the crimes that did occur. Would it be, by any chance, possible that they have an impact upon whether they are of a systematic and widespread nature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, certainly if the majority of municipalities were peaceful and a minority were not, that would influence how widespread and systematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, before the Judge's question, you tried to speculate as to what may have influenced things and how. Why speculate, if you have Prime Minister Djeric's instruction before you? In his instructions on the work of the crisis staffs, did Prime Minister Djeric aid, abet, or instigate or order crimes, or was the situation just the opposite?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In his instructions, Djeric does not aid, abet, or instigate or order crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he provide instructions against crimes, against violations of the humanitarian law and so on and so forth? You established that his instructions were implemented -- or, rather, first received and then implemented by the crisis staffs; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: His instructions do provide instructions against crimes -- against violations of humanitarian law. I do establish that his instructions were received and implemented in the municipalities. The extent of implementation -- the extent of implementation of every single article, no, I don't go through that, but I do show that they were received as an indication of the role of the crisis staffs in the state system, and I see crisis staffs operating according to these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your paragraph 45, you say: [In English] "The municipal crisis staffs co-ordinated the Serb military, political and administrative forces involved in seizing and maintaining control on the ground." [Interpretation] Let's leave "seizing and maintaining control" aside in the municipalities which were growing. Why didn't you stick to your own statement that they co-ordinated the existing structures of power? Why did you turn them into some sort of authorities beyond the existing authorities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not in paragraph 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] 145.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 145, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 145: "The municipal crisis staffs co-ordinated the Serb military ..." [Interpretation] You adhere by your statement that the crisis staffs co-ordinated Serbian military, political and administrative powers?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you establish that not even in the limited number of municipalities, you could not find the pattern? Some of the municipalities that you studied did not even have a crisis staff, and there are so many municipalities that you did not even take into account. You say, in your paragraph 67, that there was no pattern?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 67, I'm referring explicitly to the question of relations with the military, and I say that the minimum that we see everywhere is co-ordination with the military, support of the military effort. That is the common denominator. That is not in contradiction with paragraph 145, which says they co-ordinated the military, political and administrative forces. I think that's not -- I think that those are compatible. Obviously, if I was tasked to look at Bosnian Serb municipal crisis staffs, I looked at the crisis staffs. I didn't look at the municipalities where there were not crisis staffs formed, because that was not my tasking. I do note that there are some municipalities that did not form crisis staffs before March, when, in the Assembly, you called for Serb municipalities to form crisis staffs. I note that most of the crisis staffs formed in December are in the Serb minority municipalities. Again, all I can say is I'm limited to the evidence available and to my tasking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I have to ask you once again. Do you make a distinction between the crisis staffs of the party which were suggested in December and the crisis staffs of the municipalities which I referred to on the 27th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, because I saw that you did not in your speeches in 1994 and 1995 that you did not. You refer explicitly back to A and B as the basis of the municipal authorities. I see in Kljuc and Sanski Most an emphasis on the continuity. I see in many documents of these crisis staffs, their use of the SDS, even as interchangeable with the Serbian municipality, the use of the stamps interchangeably. I see continuity between the A and B crisis staffs and December crisis staffs and those operating as municipal authorities in the spring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, did you note the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce P12; English 2, Serbian 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see what, on the 14th February, the day after the beginning of the Conference on Bosnia, I said about the same things that you are talking about. The document number is P12. We need number 2 in English. I'm going to read for you from the second paragraph in the Serbian language: "We hope that the deputies are stepping up their activity in the municipalities, because as we concluded the last time, representatives is authority for a party and parties are a service to elected people, to the people and to people, elected by the people to carry out -- to carry out the political will of the people."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... passages in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "To carry out the political will of the people." So: Party officials are not authority to us. Authority for us are, first of all, the representatives, then representatives in municipal assemblies and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you neglect the fact that a party is not power, but only a service to the people who elected them?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think I neglected that. In my report, I note that in the period January to March, while the SDS deputies were creating the organs and institutions of the Bosnian Serb state, the emphasis was on the role of the Assembly deputies as the link back to the municipalities. As we know, they were to be on the crisis staffs. And you said that they must go and sit next to the president of the municipal assemblies because the president -- the municipal president is the one who actually takes action on the ground, but the Assembly deputies are to make sure that their actions are in line with SDS policy. I do emphasise the authority of the deputies there. The deputies are part of the crisis staffs. So are the municipal officials part of the crisis staffs. So I don't think that I neglected that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Let's look at D034, and let's see what I referred to on the 27th of March, when I asked the municipalities to form their crisis staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the previous document, you see that power consists of representatives, deputies, and other elected people, whereas the party and the crisis staffs only helped them, they act as their service. The deputies and representatives who were elected by the people constitute the real power. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputies made up the Bosnian Serb republican-level assembly which, as I said, set up the organs of the Bosnian Serb state. But to say that they are the only power, that ignores the entire municipal structure, also ignores the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So, no, I can't agree that only SDS deputies to the Bosnian Serb Assembly are the only power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I have mentioned everybody; deputies in the municipalities and others, secretaries, and so on and so forth. What I was trying to emphasise is that a party people were not the power, but just a service. But it's very difficult for you to understand that, Ms. Hanson, I believe. We have not got the right document. It has to be 65 ter 1000. Maybe it will be easier to get the right document in this way. D304, 304. There's something wrong with my articulation, obviously. Serbian, 33; English, 20, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will be reading for you: [In English] "When you returned ..." [Interpretation] In English, it's in the middle of the page. I'm going to read now: "When you returned to your municipalities, especially the newly-formed municipalities, I ask you to do what you are required and entitled to do under the law. The moment you arrive in your municipalities, you must urgently establish crisis staffs. You must try to organise the people so that they can defend themselves." And so on and so forth. Do you note here that I am referring to the law here? Why didn't you check what law was I referring to in here?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that you are referring to the law. As I said, I have checked the laws and did not find any reference to crisis staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Madam, did you find a law pursuant to which a municipality is entitled to carry out measures in emergencies? Why didn't you ask yourself, What law did Karadzic have in mind here?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicate in my section on the legislative origins, I thought the law you were referring to was regarding municipal presidencies or all people's defence committees. The question, though, is how much -- whether the law allowed for, for example, the formation of Serbian municipalities, and how much the law -- the letter of the law was your main motivation here. I see you appealed to the law. I didn't inquire into the legality, under the existing legal system, of each step, because I do not say that the formation of crisis staffs, themselves, was a crime. I take no stand on that. I describe the process of how they were formed, but whether they were legal or not I see as not as important as what they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I don't quite follow that. I don't. Please help me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be that crisis staffs were, indeed, provided for under the legislation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but it doesn't follow that if they -- which I haven't seen, as I emphasised, I haven't seen that. But the relationship between the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the actions of the crisis staffs set up in self-declared Serbian municipalities, even if there is a legal basis for them - we certainly see there's a legal basis for municipal presidency - that doesn't change whether the actions they took that contributed to the crimes occurring -- it doesn't mean that their actions were legal, even if they had a legal basis. You can have a legally-elected president who commits -- and I'm not -- that was just an example, I'm not referring to Dr. Karadzic in this case, but of any country -- who commits crimes, but even if he's legally elected, he can still commit a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Well, let's look at how all that looked like in Bosanski Novi, which is a municipality that you mentioned. Could the Court please produce --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 6733.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please pay attention to this document. This is a report on the work of the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Bosanski Novi. Look at the second paragraph, where it says: "The other significant issues and questions which were not easy to answer at the time was, for example --" It has to be the following page in English. And where it says: "On the 20th of April, a part of Novska Battalion," still the JNA, "that was stationed in Jasenovac, under the command of Veljko Risojevic, came to Bosanski Novi and raised Serbian flag at certain spots in the town, forcibly and under the threat of arms." And now I'm just giving you my interpretation. You can see that the Crisis Staff opposed that. And then it says: "On the 4th of May, concrete talks started with the representatives of the SDA with regard to the current political situation." The war had been going on for a month already, and they were still talking to the SDA; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says they're talking to the SDA.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the second page in Serbian, the third in English. I believe that you have already moved on to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then it says: "A curfew was introduced between 10.00 in the evening and 5.00 in the morning, and all the unlawfully-armed individuals and paramilitaries were invited to immediately, and not later than 11 May 1992, surrender their weapons either to the Municipal TO Staff or to the SJB. After that dead-line, searches," it says here -- People were not being disarmed along the ethnic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the interpreters are following at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It's very difficult to find the passage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course. Could you check the transcript and start again from the part they missed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "The curfew between 22 and 05 hours was introduced, and all the unlawfully-armed individuals and paramilitaries were invited to immediately, and no later than 11 May 1992, surrender their weapons either to the Municipal TO Staff or to the SJB. After this dead-line has passed, the searches will be carried out, with the application of force." Ms. Hanson, are they issuing this appeal to just one ethnic community? What was the basis for the surrender of weapons? Was it the ethnic background of those who held them or was it the fact that they had been unlawfully obtained?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this text, they do not mention any ethnic criteria. In practice, I believe, in many municipalities, that was not the case in practice, but the terminology used in this public report does not give any ethnic criteria, simply the question of how the arms were -- whether they were illegally armed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let us stick to the subject, Ms. Hanson. Now we're not talking about other municipalities. We're talking about these municipalities. And you have seen that the Crisis Staff opposed the Serb from the JNA who hoisted a Serbian flag over the municipality, and you see that it's not only the Muslims who are invited to surrender the weapons, but all of those who possess them illegally. Have we agreed about that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see page 4 in English about negotiations. I'm retelling it. Every time when representatives of the SDA -- it's midway through the paragraph: "In the implementation of the government's decision on disarming, every time the SDA representatives demonstrated their readiness to make it a success. However, it turned out that they either had little influence on the Muslim people or they were working on a double track, saying one thing at the negotiations, then saying something completely different to their supporters and members." Can we see page 5 in English. You will see in this paragraph: "On the 11th of May ..." That's how it begins. No, it's the same page. Oh, sorry. The beginning is on page 4. There was some shoot-out by the military police, and the Crisis Staff criticises that: "Pursuant to an order by the Crisis Staff issued around 1800 hours on the 11th of May, a cease-fire was ordered." Next page in English. And it says: "On the 12th of May, the commander of the TO Municipal Staff presented the current situation and said that TO Staff did not issue any order to open fire at Bosanski Novi, except for Blagaj, where warning shots were fired when the military police was attacked." It was his assessment that he is unable to control the entire territory of the municipalities because certain groups are distancing themselves from the chain of command and not obeying orders, and are acting on their own initiative. "Such large numbers of armed people should be placed under control."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does Mr. Karadzic have a question for Ms. Hanson? He's just reading text into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it he's going to ask a question very soon. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, let me just finish this paragraph, and then I'll come up with a question: "Simultaneously, other armed groups are appearing that hold themselves out to be regular units, army or police. But in reality, they are under nobody's control and they are looting. "After this analysis of the situation, the Crisis Staff distanced itself from the activities by all such illegal groups and paramilitary formations." That was the conclusion dated 13 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you observe, Ms. Hanson, and did you put it in your report that there had been groups under nobody's control, and that the Crisis Staff disowned and said that they need to be placed under control?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not put that in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the war in Croatia had only just finished, if at all, and that all over that territory there were many people milling around, carrying their weapons from that war, because Bosanski Novi is just on the border with Croatia? Perhaps the Trial Chamber doesn't know that.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that many troops were withdrawn from Croatia into Bosnia at this time. Many units withdrew and were relocated in Bosnia. But people milling around, carrying weapons, I find that difficult to address directly. But, yes, we see that in several municipalities, that the return of troops, largely Serb, from Croatia raised tensions in many municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was the local Muslim population armed, and did the Muslims also have their own uncontrolled elements or were they under somebody's control?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document indicates that the Muslims did have arms. It doesn't give an indication of what kind or how many, nor does it give an indication of whether they were under somebody's control. As I said, the troops that were returning were largely Serb and had been armed by the JNA, came back as JNA units. Most Muslims did not respond to the call-up for the war in Croatia, so they were not getting arms from the JNA. I have no basis to answer whether they were uncontrolled or under somebody's control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see English page 6 and Serbian 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says nicely here all these organs were ordered, and that's at the beginning of page 4 in Serbian, and the beginning of the paragraph is after the analysis of that situation. These organs were ordered and authorised to disable the work of such illegal persons and remove them from the territory of the municipality. Further below, it says: "With the involvement of the military police and the Banja Luka Corps, to assess the situation and search the terrain, including incidents in Urije town." And then it enumerates other places along the Japra River Valley where order needs to be restored. And then it says: "The assignments given by the Crisis Staff have not been implemented. Field reports say that TO armed forces are not under the control and subordination of the TO Municipal Staff Command." End of that paragraph: "TO forces must be placed under strict control of the superior command, and all instances ..." That's actually page 7 in English. "... and all instances of violation of discipline and misconduct shall be severely punished." And below that: "The Government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina belatedly sent instructions to all municipalities." In our municipality, it was received on the 20th of May. It was sent on the 26th of April, but arrived on the 20th of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what this report says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see Serbian page 5 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for indicating where the passage is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: ... all these are officials, members of the municipal government, deputy president, commander of the Territorial Defence. And then number 9: "Milan Radulovic, in charge of war crimes and damage." Do you know the Crisis Staff appointed a special officer for war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that here. I note that municipalities were charged to investigate war crimes against Serbs. There's no indication here of the ethnic -- of any ethnic criteria for the war crimes, perpetrators or victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where did you find it, that investigations were made only into crimes against Serbs? Are you perhaps confusing the Documentation and Investigation Centre in the Federal Bosnia and Herzegovina with the regular police work in investigating all crimes?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm thinking of the instructions from the member of the Presidency, Biljana Plavsic, to investigate and document war crimes against Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll find that very soon. Ms. Hanson, do you accept that the Serbian police was not able to investigate crimes in territories controlled by the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a documentation centre was established for that purpose, headed by a literary man, not a lawyer, Miroslav Toholj, to document and investigate what the police was unable to?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of the Documentation Centre, I've heard of Miroslav Toholj. What that centre was charged with and whether it was what the police were unable to do, I have no basis to answer that question. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D3585 briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, we are expected, and you are expected, and everyone who is dealing with this legal case is expected to precisely determine this: The Documentation Centre for investigating crimes in other territories is not the same as investigating on your own territory; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know enough about the Documentation Centre to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the centre, headed by Toholj, was a documentation centre, not an investigation centre; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know enough about the centre to answer questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at paragraph 2 here. Do you agree that these are instructions from the Ministry of the Interior, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sent to centres in Banja Luka, Bijeljina, Doboj, Sarajevo, Trebinje? Paragraph 2 reads: "A questionnaire will be completed at security services centres for all persons, regardless of ethnicity (Muslims, Croats, Serb, et cetera) against whom criminal reports are filed because of reasonable suspicion that they are responsible for crimes." This is an instruction on the documentation and investigation of war crimes, as we can see in paragraph 1. And in paragraph 2, it says: "Without discrimination." Have you read this? Why do you keep maintaining the Serbs investigated only crimes against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not in my report because it's not about crisis staffs. I do not state in my report, as far as I can recall, that -- I don't enter into the question of police investigations into war crimes or crimes. That wasn't in -- I didn't find that in the scope of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But, Madam, you invoke wrongly Biljana Plavsic, who asked that this be documented, and here the police is required to investigate, regardless of faith and nationality. You are misstating facts in an attempt to support the theory about Serbian culpability.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no theory about Serbian culpability. There are individuals charged. The nation is not charged. I talk about the Bosnian Serb leadership, and I don't like being accused of just -- of blaming all Serbs. Yes, I agree, this document says "to investigate all the crimes, regardless of nationality." I do believe that there is a document from Biljana Plavsic. I didn't include it in my report because it wasn't addressed specifically to crisis staffs. Perhaps it will come up somewhere -- some other time in the course of the trial. I wasn't talking about this document when I mentioned the one from Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted? I don't have time to ask you whether this minister was part of the Bosnian Serb leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this minister part of the Bosnian Serb leadership, Mr. Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the previous Bosanski Novi document has been already admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was P2632, if I'm correct. And we'll admit this as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D1360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If this document has been admitted, let me ask you, Madam: Are you aware of this document, and do you agree that in here the Crisis Staff - Serbian page 6, English 9 - says that its orders have not been honoured and that complete chaos occurred? It straddles pages 8 and 9 in English and pages 5 and 6 in Serbian. Can we get back that previous document, 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2632, the previous one about Bosanski Novi; Serbian page 5, English 8. Serbian 5, English 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This deals with the problems in the Japra River Valley, the sectoral TO Staff for Agic, Rujinka and Krsalj, Muslim-populated places, turned a deaf ear to the endeavours of the official policies and organs of the authorities and started to deal with things on their own. Then a conflict started and expulsion of Muslim civilians from one village to another village. And: "The Crisis Staff reacted vigorously and issued an order to the Municipal TO Staff that they should immediately place all their members and units under their control ..." So it says here the order was not followed. And on pages 6, English 9, it says: "Complete chaos has begun to reign." Ms. Hanson, in your footnote 162, you characterise these events in Bosanski Novi as ethnic cleansing, led by the Crisis Staff, whereas you have evidence that the Crisis Staff is warning against chaos and issuing orders completely contrary to what you describe. It's paragraph 99, I believe, and footnote 169 in your report. That's what you say: [In English] "Examples of crisis staffs actually setting forced deportation as a policy include:" [Interpretation] And you say "Bosanski Novi" among them, Blagaj, the Japra River Valley. So you ascribe this chaos, you blame it on a deliberate process controlled by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter from the president of the Crisis Staff, Radomir Pasic, to the population of the Japra Valley says, If you don't move out, we can't guarantee your safety, which caused a lot of people to move out, thinking that the authority -- the municipal authorities refused to guarantee their safety, or were unable to guarantee their safety, perhaps. But I think if you consider the people being held in the stadium at this time, the discussions with UNPROFOR and others to help the Muslims of Novi, that you have to understand a report like this, which was written to be adopted by the Municipal Assembly when the Crisis Staff finished its work, involves a lot of passing the blame on. A lot of these reports sort of say, Crimes happened, but it wasn't us, things were out of our control. They may be true, they may not. It's part -- it's part of the whole context and setting here. Yes, Pasic says, It was out of our control. He says that here. He threatened the Muslims that if they didn't leave, he couldn't guarantee their safety. Whether this was forced or voluntary depends on your view of the context, and I do not entirely trust the language of reports like this when they are endeavouring to cast blame elsewhere. I see this kind of language in a lot of the -- when I rely on documents written by the crisis staffs, themselves, I focus on what they say they did. The whys can be less credible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Ms. Hanson, your task was to present all the facts to the Trial Chamber, and then the Trial Chamber can decide whether they are credible or not. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: All facts? No. The Trial Chamber will be hearing, I believe -- I don't know -- I don't even remember what's charged in Bosanski Novi because I'm not familiar with the current state of the indictment, but I imagine the Trial Chamber will also be hearing from other people about events in Bosanski Novi. My job was to present documents, not the whole story that is unavailable in the documents of the crisis staffs or contemporary records at the time. I am not supposed to be presenting material outside of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Madam, we are going around and around. Despite what you say, that you are supposed to present documents, you have not presented documents. You did not take into account the chaos of war and the efforts of the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Novi to restore order and peace. You characterised it in a certain way. You made a judgement that the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Novi controlled the situation and led the expulsions of Bosnian Muslims. And with a selective way, you treat documents. What you are doing is you are being very selective and you are deciding for yourself which ones to believe and which not.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of my job, as an analyst, is not to believe every document on its face value. I do cite this document. I read it. But noting that the Crisis Staff did have the forces and the ability to secure a convoy of people to leave the municipality, but they didn't seem to have the ability to protect those people within the municipality, I did not believe all of the justifications they cite in this report. Previously, in my first report, all the documents on which I relied were also given to the Court, and I'm very glad to have as many documents as possible made available to the Court. The process changed because there were a lot of documents. The more documents the Court can see, the better they can draw their own conclusions. But I also note that this report starts out, right at the beginning, discussing how the Crisis Staff was formed on the instructions of the Main Board of the SDS. So I rely more on what they say they did than their motivations for it. When I rely only on documents written by crisis staffs, there's a lot of, let's say, blaming others, protecting themselves. These are documents issued for the whole municipality to be discussed at the Municipal Assembly. I don't think crisis staffs usually say, We did all this. They don't list everything they do, and they're not always honest about what they -- why they did it. I hope the Court will hear more evidence of events in Bosanski Novi in which they'll be able to put this document in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that crisis staffs are misinforming their own leadership?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they're submitting their reports to the municipal assemblies, I think they -- or in their own minutes, I think they choose words to make themselves look as good as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I note the time. Can I be given at least another half an hour, because there is a clear gap between my needs and with what I have been able to achieve. And if you given me another half an hour, I may be able to just fill in some of that gap. If I'm able to finish before that half an hour expires, I'll try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that you haven't wasted time today, and that as long as you remain on relevant issues, we'll grant that. We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 5915 is the next document I would like to call up. It should have a translation. This is a Prosecutor's number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you speak Serbian, and Croatian as well. Do you agree that the president of the Republic of Croatia, President Tudjman, issued a decision on crisis staffs on the 27th of August, 1991? And in here, in Article 1, he says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the accused is reading too fast and we don't have a translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are simply reading too fast, without any translated material. Could you slow down and repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Decision on Crisis Staffs," which was issued on the 27th of August, 1991: "The Government of the Republic of Croatia, in keeping with its constitutional obligations and authorities, is duty-bound to ensure a co-ordinated action of executive and administrative bodies of the state authorities in the republic, as well as economic and social activities, in conditions when the independence of the republic is threatened or in the state of war, as well as the logistics support and all the other assistance to the commands and units of the armed forces. For that purpose, the Government of the Republic of Croatia forms the Crisis Staff of the Republic of Croatia, as well as the crisis staffs as co-ordinating bodies."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is what it says in this article?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me not read the rest of it. Do you agree that the second paragraph of Article 2 says that in terms of their position -- or, rather, by virtue of their position, government members and ministers are also members of the Crisis Staff? And the last sentence says: "The Government of the Republic of Croatia can appoint up to three other members of the Crisis Staff who are not its members already by virtue of their position." Right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it say in Article 3: "In the municipalities in which the local bodies of authorities regularly perform their duties and are loyal to the Republic of Croatia, the president of the Municipal Crisis Staff is also the president of the Executive Council of the municipality, and its members are the heads of municipal administrative bodies." And so on and so forth. Do you agree that he cannot form crisis staffs in the municipalities which are not loyal to the republic, but only in the republics which are obedient, which are loyal to the republican authorities? Right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Article 4 says: "In order to co-ordinate the work and activities of the municipal crisis staffs, the Government of the Republic of Croatia can form a crisis staff that will cover a territory of several municipalities or it can appoint its own commissioner that will be in charge of several municipalities." Do you agree that they also have an institution -- or, rather, that they have the institution of a commissioner who helps municipalities in an attempt to co-ordinate their activities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Municipalities, themselves, can also appoint commissioners for local communes or settlements, and so on and so forth; right? Do you agree that a crisis staff is just a form through which the existing authorities function, rather than an entirely new body?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar enough with the Croatian legislation to really draw that. I see here it refers to that the Executive Committee of the Assembly can form a crisis staff or name a -- oh, the commissioner is just to the local levels. That is so different from the model that I've seen in the Bosnian Serb municipalities that I'm really reluctant to draw any conclusions without having studied the Croatian legislation better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read Article 5, where it says: "When this decision comes into force, the decision on the setting up and activities of the Crisis Staff in the Republic of Croatia, number 822/91 of 29 July 1999, will become null and void, as well as all the decisions --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The text has just disappeared from the screen, and the accused was reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we can all read this document later on, when it's translated. What is your question on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Ms. Hanson, when we look at your footnote, and when we see that you say that the crisis staffs existed elsewhere, can we now finally underline the fact that those crisis staffs, indeed, existed and that they existed much before the Serbian crisis staffs were ever set up?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date of this was August. Yes, had I realised in my writing how much other crisis staffs -- non-Serb crisis staffs would matter to the readers of my report on Bosnian Serb crisis staffs, I would have expanded that section to make it clear that we hear of crisis staffs in Croatia in 1991. We see crisis staffs on the Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Government side as well. I readily can see I did not pay attention to it -- much attention to that in my report on Bosnian Serb municipal crisis staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect, Ms. Hanson, the crisis staffs that were formed by the Muslim side in January 1991, only a month after our elections, were not the staffs of the Bosnian government. They were, rather, the staffs of the Muslim community. The Crisis Staff of the Bosnian Presidency was formed in mid-September 1991. In any case, all of them had crisis staffs much before the first Serbian crisis staffs were set up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've listened to an intercept from, I believe, June 1991, in which you say there is an SDS crisis staff already. It's not in my report because it wasn't a municipal one, but I have heard mention of a Serbian SDS crisis staff from the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that conversation, I'm trying to calm down somebody who was putting pressure on me to form a crisis staff. Did a crisis staff exist at the time I indicated in my question?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your question, what -- I'm sorry, what time do you -- do you refer to, what time-period?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1991. Did it exist in the summer of 1991? Did the Crisis Staff exist at the time that I indicated?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, I've only your word for it in that intercept. That's the only indication I have of a republic-level SDS crisis staff in the summer of 1991. I have no other documents regarding that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, very well. Do you know that people on the ground in municipalities formed crisis staffs whenever they felt that there was a crisis coming, even before the instructions were issued in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say in my report, I have seen or heard references to ad-hoc crisis staffs formed even before -- well, before the war, I've seen references, I know, to a crisis staff for the reception of refugees in Bosanski Petrovac, I believe, in the summer of 1991, refugees coming from Croatia. So I have heard the term used, but not as a municipal government organ; simply a co-ordinating body to deal with a specific issue or local crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do we have a 65 ter or the exhibit number of the intercept she has referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was just trying to work out which one it was myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If Ms. Hanson can tell me the speakers, if she's able.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other speaker's name is Zoran -- I'm afraid that's all it is, Zoran. I believe it's June 1991. If I may explain, Your Honours, I listened to intercepts in which the word "crisis staff" appeared, so I don't know if they're on the exhibit list or not. I was doing my own researches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the previous document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court produce 65 ter 594, only in English, because the Serbian version is a handwritten document. Page 11, please. As for the previous question, the instructions were issued in December 1992; page 43, line 23. The instructions were issued in December 1991. The month was not recorded the first time 'round.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at bullet point 3, where it says: [In English] "From the second session of the Municipal Board of SDS Bratunac, held on the 25th of October, 1991." [Interpretation] Can we go to the following page. Bullet point 3: [In English] "Appointment of the Crisis Staff of Bratunac municipality for implementation of measures for protection of the Serbian people." [Interpretation] Do you agree with me that those people of Bratunac acted of their own will and that they formed a crisis staff independently, even before the instructions were issued in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is obviously before the 19 December instructions. But if we can look at item 1, it follows information from the Main Board of the SDS. If we can go back to the previous page. "Information on the standpoints of the Main Board of the SDS BiH and the standpoints and conclusions of the newly-elected Serbian Assembly of the BiH." In my report, I tie this Crisis Staff to the declaration of a state of emergency in the party which Mr. Karadzic gave on the 18th, I believe, October. And if this is the same one -- could I just go to the top of this document? What's the date of it? It's the -- yeah, because I also -- I cite a document from the 19th of October in which Deronjic informs the leaders of the SDS Municipal Board of Bratunac of the policies and instructions from the expanded session of the SDS Main Board held the night before in Sarajevo: "The membership of the municipal crisis staff was proposed immediately." And the Bratunac crisis staff then met on the 26th of October. So, actually, the day after this party emergency was declared, Deronjic comes back to Bratunac and says, We got instructions from the SDS leadership, and therefore a crisis staff should be formed. I tie that to the state of party emergency. I agree it is formed before the 19 December instructions, but I would not say that it's completely on their own initiative. The explicit references to instructions and information from the party centre make me think it was not completely an initiative. They may have jumped the gun, perhaps, already hearing of this term "crisis staff," forming a crisis staff, given that the party is declared to be in a state of emergency, but I think that they were -- that they were seeing themselves as following the party line at that time. I also see, in Bosanski Petrovac at this same time in late October, the SDS Municipal Board proposes forming a crisis staff, which the Municipal Assembly, being still a multi-ethnic body, rejects. So I think there may have been talk of a crisis staff or the declaration on the state of emergency may have led people to use this term "crisis staff." I see no written instructions at this time from the party centre about a crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This document has been admitted. Could the Court please produce 1D3594.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would ask you to help me go quickly through the following few documents. There is not much left for us to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the previous document was Exhibit P2597.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that this was issued on the 16th of January, 1992, and that these are decisions of the Presidency of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina? And we can go immediately to the second page, both in English and in Croatian. I don't want to say "Serbian." I would like to draw your attention and everybody's attention to bullet point 7 and 8, where it says: "Crisis staffs of the HDZ of BH at all levels ..." And so on and so forth. Were you familiar with this document? This was signed by the president of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Stjepan Kljuic, a member of the Joint Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, it was signed by Kljuic, who was a member of the Joint Presidency. I was not familiar with this document at the time I wrote my report. It was brought to my attention since then, but I don't feel it changes my conclusions on Bosnian Serb municipal crisis staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you come across a document which indicates that Plavsic/Koljevic did the same, that they managed the area as members of the Joint Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what you mean by "managed the area," but I have not seen an equivalent document like this from Plavsic or Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted? This is precisely what I meant. You understood me well. It was a good equivalent of what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have five minutes, Mr. Karadzic. We dealt with Croatian crisis staff yesterday, which was noted in her footnote 5. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I have to skip over so many things, and I have to ask you this: You are appearing today as an expert witness, or, rather, you have testified here as an expert witness; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you still affiliated with the OTP, are you still a staff member there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is your capacity as a staff member in the OTP? You are a researcher, you're not an investigator; right? You are a research officer; that's what you told us?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the name of my post is "research officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When your testimony is finished today, you are going back to your work to be a research officer; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hope I get a short break, but, yes, on Monday I'll start.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're going to try to help the OTP to reinforce their case against me; right?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to try to help the OTP to better their case, which includes a better understanding, if necessary, of all sides of the issues. But, yes, I will go back to working to help the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have also stated that you did the same in the Krajisnik case. Before you provided evidence, you were a research officer, and you had collected documents that supported the Prosecution case. And then you were transformed into an independent expert witness, and you remained that for the duration of your testimony. And after that, you were again transformed or you went back to being a research officer and an associate of the OTP. Right? You said that on page 14721, from line 1 onwards. I can look for that.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you feel the need. But I agree with that statement, so I'm not challenging you to find it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Hanson, do you find it difficult to turn from a research officer, and an associate of the OTP, into an impartial expert witness? How difficult is it to go back and forth between these roles?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It requires some intellectual rigour to separate -- to separate the roles, but I -- my report -- my work is based on the documents, and I have faith that the documents show what I'm saying. And I do try and keep out other sources when I testify, when I write my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I put it to you, Ms. Hanson, that Mr. Krajisnik was found guilty of only one charge in the indictment, and that is persecution of the Muslim population, and that the decision was based mainly on your findings, on the results of your research, and at the same time if I tell you that he is a totally innocent person, how will that make you feel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, an improper comment. I take it you concluded your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was not a comment. I asked Ms. Hanson whether she feels responsible for the fact that an innocent man was convicted based on such a selective approach to work. Okay, I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, it's a blatant comment, thinly disguised as a question. We both know it's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And not helpful at all. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, a moment ago you asked for the 65 ter number for the intercept that Ms. Hanson was referring to. If I could call up 65 ter 30073, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, this is an intercept between Mr. Karadzic and a man called Zoran on the 29th of June, 1991. Is this the intercept that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. On the second page, Karadzic says: "We have a crisis staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that document, Your Honour, to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He also connects it to a secret. He says, We have a crisis staff, but we can't tell them about secrets over the phone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be MFI P2713.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: While we're on the subject of intercepts, I have another one from June 1991. If I could have Exhibit 65 ter 30035, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, this is an intercept of a conversation between Dobrica Cosic and Radovan Karadzic on the 8th of June, 1991. Have you reviewed this intercept?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but it's not -- I'm not recognising it right now. It's still just -- the first pages are just the usual chitchat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 12 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S. I'm sorry, page 8 of the English. In the bottom right-hand corner, it says "8th of --" thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just at the top of the page, do you recall reviewing this intercept, now that you see that text?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what's the significance of that in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Krupa and Sanski Most are already planning to establish a Serbian municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that and ask that it be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI P2714, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, at page 33/34 of today's transcript, Mr. Karadzic took you to Exhibit D1360, which was the Mico Stanisic document. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that you had seen documents which referred to only investigating crimes against the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 09342 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a strictly-confidential dispatch from the minister, Mico Stanisic, to the CSBs Banja Luka, Bijeljina, Doboj, Sarajevo and Trebinje. Is this a document that you may have reviewed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've seen this one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it states in the first paragraph -- and it's dated, sorry, the 16th of May, 1992: "In view of the tasks resulting from the order by the minister of the interior, Strictly Confidential number," and gives the number, "and for the purpose of monitoring combat operations and regular activities of the organs of the interior, and in order to collect documentation on the crimes against the Serbian population (for prosecution and to accurately inform the local and international public), fax reports must be submitted daily to the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Did you -- do you recall seeing other similar documents to this?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I've seen something from Plavsic with similar instructions to collect documentation on crimes against the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it we have a full translation of this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2715.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, Mr. Karadzic took you to -- on Wednesday, at the end of the session, to Exhibit D01356, which is a report by the SDS Municipal Board in Prijedor. Do you recall seeing that document? It was the report written in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the SDS Municipal Board. Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And during -- looking at that report, he was making the point that there was no communication between the Prijedor SDS and the republic-level SDS. And then he, at transcript page 14788, said: "Well, we looked a moment ago at a diary that we looked at." I'm sorry, the diary was D01356, the Prijedor Municipal Board report was D01357. In any event, he said: "Well, the diary we looked at a little while ago, if we had time, we would point your attention to where it says that they had not had contact for 45 days with the representatives from Prijedor." THE COURT REPORTER: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him referring to a 45-day break in communications, with no reference to -- without bringing up a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check whether the transcript reflects all of what you asked to the witness?
